units: the craftswoman answers her student's questions about the fabrics in the workroom
she names first a light fiber used for warm-season shirts
she describes a second, rougher fiber meant for sacks and aprons
she states that a short-pile cloth swallows the light and suits ceremonial jackets
she points out that a pressed material never frays and spares the finishing of edges
she buys in narrow strips an openwork cloth that she fastens onto collars
the openwork cloth is the most expensive because it demands a patient hand
she asserts that the choice of a material depends on the purpose of the garment
she announces that the student will know the fabrics by touch before knowing them by sight
text: The seamstress fields her student's questions about the cloth stacked on the shelves around the workroom. Linen comes first: cool against the skin, easy to drape, and saved for the shirts worn through the warm months. Hemp comes next, coarser under the fingers, the fiber she reaches for when she cuts sacks and aprons. Velvet, she says, swallows the light instead of throwing it back, and it suits a jacket meant for ceremony. Felt never frays at the cut, so nobody has to finish its edges. Last she names lace, which she buys in narrow strips and stitches onto collars. Her student asks which one costs the most. Lace, by a wide margin, because it demands a patient hand and a trained eye. Cloth is picked for the job it has to do, she adds, never for taste alone, and before long her student will know each one by touch sooner than by sight.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: old fabrics came from fibers drawn out of plant stems
preparing those fibers called for soaking and then beating
getting enough to clothe a single chest took several weeks
harnessing the wheel to the distaff raised output
pedal looms freed the weaver's hands
the steam engine then made the workrooms bigger
the price of a shirt fell so far that people of modest means could own two
fibers born of chemistry are the most recent stage
those recent fibers dry quickly and barely crease
text: Picture a workroom where the thread is still spun by hand, strand after strand, and you have the starting point of the whole story. Old cloth began its life as fiber stripped away from the stems of plants. You soaked it, you beat it, you combed it out, and weeks went by before you had enough of it to cover a single chest. Then somebody clever hitched a wheel to the distaff, and output climbed. Pedal looms came along after that, and the weaver's hands were suddenly free for nothing but the shuttle. Steam took over next, the workrooms swelled, and the price of a shirt dropped so low that people of modest means could keep two of them at once. The latest turn you are probably wearing right now: thread that came out of chemistry, which dries again in no time and stubbornly refuses to crease.

units: the wearing out of a shoe follows mechanical causes
the foot rolls its weight from back to front
that way of bearing down wears the heel first and then the toe
the thinning of the outer layer removes the cushioning
the unabsorbed shock travels up to the knee joint
hard surfaces speed up the breakdown of the sole
a sole soaked with water loses its shape and its stiffness
makers stack layers of unequal density
the writer concludes that the stride wears the shoe more than the material does
text: A shoe wears out along mechanical lines, and never at random. The foot rolls its weight from the back toward the front, so the sole meets friction unevenly: the heel goes first and the toe follows behind it. Once the outer layer thins away, the cushioning is gone and the shock climbs straight up to the knee joint, which is why steady walkers ache there. Hard surfaces speed the whole process up, since the ground gives back nothing of what it takes. Water makes matters worse. A sole soaked through swells out of shape, loses its stiffness, and lets the foot slide around inside. Makers answer by stacking up layers of unequal density, firm underneath and softer on top. That holds up far better, though the principle stands: it is the stride that wears the shoe, not the material.

units: a tear damages the front of a borrowed dress
the dress has to be returned the next day
an edge-to-edge seam would have left a visible mark on the satin
the idea of hiding the tear under a belt is dropped
a neighbor who once kept a sewing supplies shop examines the cloth
the neighbor suggests adding an embroidered motif rather than mending
the embroidered motif shows a stem and three leaves
the owner of the dress notices the motif and asks where it was bought
text: A tear the width of a fingernail ran across the front of the borrowed dress, and the woman who had to hand the thing back the next day felt her throat tighten. Drawing the edges together would have left a ridge on the pale satin, plain to anyone. She thought of hiding the whole thing under a belt, then gave that up, since the waist sat too high. The neighbor across the landing, who had once kept a shop for sewing supplies, turned the cloth toward the window and studied it. Her idea was not to mend but to add: pale thread, a stem and three leaves, laid exactly over the wound in the satin. The work took up a whole evening, the needle moving along without hurry. The owner stopped short at the motif the next day and asked where it had been bought. Not for sale, came the answer.

units: the choice of a fastening system depends on the intended use
the lace runs through metal rings and spreads the tension over the whole height
the lace adjusts finely and can be replaced for a trifling sum
the lace calls for slow handling and comes undone if the knot is loosely tied
the metal clasp shuts in one motion and holds without supervision
the metal clasp imposes a fixed width that does not follow changes of measurement
lacing is advised for a work garment worn over layers of varying thickness
the metal clasp is advised for a formal jacket because it stays discreet
the edge must be reinforced against pulling before assembly
text: Before you settle on lacing or clasps, look hard at what the garment has to do. A lace threads through metal eyelets and spreads the pull evenly all the way up the opening. It tunes finely, and replacing one costs next to nothing. The drawback is handling: lacing is slow, and a knot pulled loosely will work itself open. A clasp shuts in a single motion and stays shut with no attention at all, but it locks you into one width, so the garment stops following the body once the measurement shifts. For work clothing, choose the lace, because the tension has to change with the thickness of whatever is worn underneath. For a formal jacket, the clasp keeps out of sight and leaves the front undistorted. Either way, check that the edge is braced against pulling before you set the lining in.

units: a trade gathering devoted to fabrics has just ended
the organizers single out four announcements
a group of workshops claims it can break cutting scraps back into fiber and feed them into fresh yarn
a woven label will state the origin of the fiber and the place of dyeing
several retail chains pledge to make the list of their subcontractors public
a machine now trims the selvedge without scorching it
that trimming does away with the hard ridge the sewers had to remove
the exhibitors expect these pledges to turn into firm orders
text: A trade gathering devoted to cloth came to a close last night, and its organizers single out four announcements from it. The first concerns recycling: a group of workshops says it can break cutting scraps back down to fiber and feed them into fresh yarn without weakening it. The second covers traceability, since every piece will now carry a woven label naming where the fiber was grown and where it was dyed. The third bears on manufacturing conditions, with several retail chains pledging to publish the list of their subcontractors. The fourth is quieter and speaks mainly to technicians: one machine now trims the selvedge without scorching it, which does away with the hard ridge that sewers used to cut off separately. Exhibitors are waiting to see the pledges turn into firm orders.

units: a coat hanging near the door changes its look as the seasons pass
at the end of the cold season the velvet collar bears the mark of the scarf
the pile of the collar stays flattened in one direction
during the mild season the garment is brushed and then stored in a cotton bag
the cotton bag takes away its smell of smoke
through the hot stretch it sleeps folded on a high shelf
it is folded with the lining outward to avoid marks
a damp cloth and a warm iron erase the crease that appeared across the back
the felt hat keeps a dent for good once the dent is pressed into it
text: The coat hangs from a hook beside the door, and it does not look the same from one season to the next. At the close of the cold months, the velvet collar still shows the place where the scarf pressed down on it: the pile lies flat one way and will not stand back up. The mild weeks arrive, and the coat is brushed, aired out, then hung inside a cotton bag, where the smell of smoke gradually leaves it. Through the hottest stretch it sleeps folded on a high shelf, the lining turned outward so that nothing marks the face of the cloth. When the chill comes back, out it comes with a sharp crease running across the back, which a damp cloth and a warm iron eventually smooth away. The felt hat above it goes through the same round, but forgives less: a dent pressed into it stays for good.

units: the writer is irritated by the flimsiness of mass-produced clothing
the seams give way at the second wash and the linings split
the customer buys again the garment he has just worn out
the labels have found that fast turnover pays better than durability
makers cut the weight of the cloth and drop the reinforcements at the stress points
an alterations shop now turns down certain repairs for lack of solid material
the writer notes that customers accept a shirt lasting a single season
the writer believes the change will come from the piled-up cost of failed purchases
text: Honestly, the state of the clothing turned out in bulk is enough to put anyone out of temper. Seams give way at the second wash, linings split open, and the buyer ends up paying twice for the very jacket he has just worn through. There is no mystery in it: the labels worked out long ago that fast turnover pays better than durability. So the cloth is made lighter, sturdy thread gives way to something thinner, and the bracing at every stress point quietly disappears. The alterations shop down the street now turns certain jobs away, because nothing is left for a needle to grip. And we adjust: a shirt that survives one season strikes us as normal. My guess is that the reckoning will come from the wallet, once the failed purchases add up to more than one garment sewn to last.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a craftsman cuts soles in a narrow room that opens onto the street
he has worked at this trade since he left school
customers had things repaired less and less often
the leather suppliers imposed lots too heavy for a single workshop
training no longer drew any candidates
he gave up closing and changed his line of work
he now makes custom wooden lasts for difficult feet
his orders come from doctors and rehabilitation therapists
he has trained two apprentices, one of whom already assembles the uppers alone
he says that the shape of the foot dictates the model and not the reverse
text: In a narrow room that opens straight onto the street, the shoemaker has been cutting soles since the day he left school. The trade nearly went out with him. Customers brought things in for repair less and less often, the leather suppliers would sell only in lots too heavy for one workshop to carry, and nobody came asking to be trained. He could have shut the door. Instead he changed what he made: rather than waiting on repairs, he turns custom wooden lasts for difficult feet, the ones that mass production rubs raw. His orders come from doctors and rehabilitation therapists now. He has trained two apprentices, and one of them already assembles the uppers on her own. Asked what he is proudest of, he points to a pair on the bench whose sole carries the print of an uneven stride, and says the foot gives the orders, never the model.

units: two dresses are displayed facing each other in a room
the first dress is cut from a dark velvet
the velvet swallows the light and falls straight
the second dress is of undyed lace and lets the air and the gaze pass through
the wall can be made out behind the openwork dress
the onlooker prefers the dark dress at first because of its mass
the judgment reverses when the eye lingers
the openwork dress displays its own drawing, in which each loop holds the next
the onlooker ends up admiring the hand that carried out the work
the heavy piece is forgotten on the way out while the light one keeps drawing the eye
text: Two dresses stand facing each other in the back room, and nothing about them agrees. The first, cut from dark velvet, drinks the light; it has weight, it falls straight, it hushes everything around it. The second, in undyed lace, lets both the air and the eye pass through, so the wall shows behind it as though the cloth were unsure it existed. At first glance the velvet wins, so plainly does its mass command the room. Then the eye lingers, and the verdict turns over. Velvet offers a surface and nothing more, while the lace lays out its own drawing, every loop holding the next with no knot in sight. In the end you admire the hand that tied it rather than the dress itself. The odd part is what you carry out: the heavy piece slips away, the light one keeps pulling you back.
